⚖️ THE LIVE WEIGHTS, ALREADY SET

This course's three Canvas assignment groups are weighted 20/30/50 and group weighting is on. The table below is how the gradebook ships.

Assignment Group Items Ships At What Lives Here
Comprehension Checks 36 20% 36 comprehension quizzes, one per lesson (1.01 to 4.09). Auto-graded, 5 multiple-choice questions each, 5 pts.
Writing Assignments 37 30% 37 items: 24 weekly Assignments and quarterly synthesis essays (100 pts each, 4-criteria rubric), 12 Warm-Ups (20 pts each, pass/fail) and 1 Discussion (lesson 1.01, 100 pts, 4-criteria rubric).
Module Capstones 14 50% 14 Module Capstones, one per module from Q1 Module 2 through Q4 Module 4 (Q1 Module 1 has none), 100 pts each, each with a 4-criteria rubric.

Also outside every weighted group, by design and not an omission: the 30 Tier 4 module intro/outro wrappers, built as true Canvas Quiz surveys (quiz_type: survey). Surveys have no associated gradebook assignment at all — unlike a 0%-weighted graded item, they carry zero gradebook footprint by construction, not by a weight set to zero.

💡 HOW THESE WEIGHTS WERE CHOSEN

This is not a straight lift of optima-canvas-assignments' 60/25/15 item-count ratio applied to grade percentages — that ratio describes workload distribution and teacher-hours, not scored value. Small classes did not generate real peer engagement on weekly Discussion boards, so the weekly Discussions were replaced by short pass/fail Warm-Ups, and each module from Week 4 on ends in one graded Capstone drawing on the whole module. The Capstones carry the most weight (50%) because they are the deepest assessment in each module; the weekly Assignments, essays and Warm-Ups together carry 30%, and the auto-graded Comprehension Checks carry 20%.

These percentages (20/30/50) are the same in both semesters. Canvas sets group weights per course, so check them in Grades → Assignment Groups after you import.

✅ IF YOU WANT TO CHANGE THIS

Adjust weights directly in Grades → Assignment Groups. Unlike the World History course, there is no single generator script tying the Canvas weights and the syllabus's Assessment & Grading section together here — if you change a group's weight, update the syllabus's grading table by hand to match, or it will drift.

Raising an individual assignment's point value only redistributes weight within its own group; it does not touch another group's percentage. To change how much Writing Assignments or Comprehension Checks count toward the overall grade, change that group's weight directly.

About this syllabus. This is the plan for the On-Demand (asynchronous) section of the course as designed. It is a full-year course; you pace through the four quarters of your enrolled year. Optima also offers this course as a Live section with the same content and expectations, described in its own syllabus. Exact pacing and a few activities may vary from term to term. Your facilitator will confirm the specifics for your section.

COURSE OVERVIEW

Philosophy Honors: Ethics is a yearlong survey of moral philosophy in the Western tradition, moving from the ancient search for moral knowledge through the major frameworks philosophers have used to answer it. Scholars begin with Plato's Euthyphro and the challenges of moral epistemology, move through utilitarian and Kantian accounts of consequence and duty, study Aristotle's virtue ethics and his account of human flourishing, and close with Aquinas's natural law tradition. Each quarter tests its framework against real objections and hard cases, and the course ends with a capstone essay comparing all four accounts of morality against one another.

WHAT SCHOLARS WILL LEARN TO DO
  • Distinguish descriptive from normative claims and identify when a genuine ethical question arises.
  • Evaluate the major challenges to moral knowledge: emotivism, moral relativism, and the fact/value gap.
  • Compare consequentialist and Kantian accounts of right action, including utilitarianism and the categorical imperative.
  • Explain Aristotle's account of eudaimonia, the virtues, and practical wisdom (phronesis).
  • Apply the doctrine of the mean and the cardinal virtues to specific cases of character.
  • Explain Aquinas's natural law theory, the doctrine of double effect, and the basic human goods.
  • Evaluate applied ethical questions in medicine, war, and emerging technology using multiple frameworks.
  • Construct and defend a reasoned position on which account of morality is most adequate.
BIG PROJECTS & MILESTONES

ON-DEMAND (ASYNCHRONOUS) LEARNING

In the On-Demand section you move through the course at your own pace within each quarter, guided by due dates that keep you on track. All assignments for a quarter open at its start and close at its end. Because the course is On-Demand, there is no grade penalty for missing an individual due date; any assignment not completed by the end of the quarter receives a zero, and assignments submitted in the final 14 days of a quarter receive a 10% deduction, so steady pacing matters.

Attendance is measured by assignment completion. Per school policy, a scholar who completes no assignment for ten consecutive school days, without notifying the school of an absence in advance, may be dropped from the course. Completion means a sincere attempt: real effort on real work. Rushed work, wrong or corrupted files, irrelevant or nonsense submissions, AI-generated filler, and word-salad responses do not count.

You are never on your own. A live facilitator grades your work, gives feedback, and hosts a weekly study hall and VR workshops.

This course is also taught as a Live (synchronous) section that meets on a schedule on Optima's VR campus. If that is the section you are enrolled in, use the Live syllabus instead of this one.

USING AI IN THIS COURSE

Optima's AI policy does not ask whether a scholar used AI. It asks whether AI was used honestly, skillfully, and in a way that genuinely built your own thinking. AI may support your work, but it may not do the reasoning an assignment asks of you.

WHICH AI TOOLS YOU MAY USE
  • Every scholar. Any AI used for this course is school-controlled: tools built into Canvas assignments and into Optima's VR platform, set up to ask you questions and prompt your thinking rather than hand you answers. No assignment in this course requires a personal AI account.
  • Scholars under 14. Your facilitator may not ask, suggest, or require that you use an AI tool outside those school-controlled platforms. Your AI work for this course happens in Canvas and in VR.
  • Scholars 14 and older. Whether you use an outside AI tool for schoolwork is your family's decision, not the school's. It requires written parent or guardian permission on file with your facilitator, and your parent or guardian selects the tool, sets up the account, monitors it, and stays responsible for it. Optima does not provide, endorse, or manage personal AI accounts. Your facilitator's part is to judge whether the AI was used well.
WHAT IS EXPECTED WHEN YOU USE AI
  • Document it. Record the tool, the prompt you gave it, and the date. Using AI is not plagiarism. Turning in AI-generated work as entirely your own thought, with no documentation, is.
  • Verify it. AI states wrong things confidently, and you are responsible for every claim you submit, so check it against a credible source before it goes into your work. Verification is one of the skills this course grades.
  • Sound like yourself. Your work should read the way you write and speak in the rest of the course, take a real position rather than hedging, and be something you can explain on the spot, on camera or in VR, when your facilitator asks a follow-up question you did not expect.
  • Keep the process, not just the product. Prompt logs, drafts, revision notes, and VR recordings are gradeable evidence of your thinking. When an assignment asks for them, they count toward your grade.

Some assignments limit or exclude AI so that you build the underlying skill yourself, and the assignment page will say so. The reason is practical: you cannot judge whether an AI's answer is any good unless you can do the work without it.

LEARNING IN VIRTUAL REALITY

Optima is a virtual-reality school. Alongside your Canvas coursework, you will join immersive sessions on Optima's VR campus, where you meet teachers and fellow scholars, take part in live activities, and explore places and ideas you could not visit in an ordinary classroom. Keep your headset charged and ready for any scheduled VR sessions, and treat the VR campus with the same courtesy and seriousness you would a physical one. If you ever cannot get into VR for a session, tell your facilitator: there is an alternative way to take part so you do not fall behind.

BEING AN OPTIMA SCHOLAR

Optima's mission is an excellent, virtue-centered education, and virtue is at the center of this course as much as any other. Every scholar is expected to practice the seven virtues that shape life at Optima: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. In practice that means: do your own honest work; treat everyone you meet in, through, or because of this course with respect, in writing, in discussion, and in VR; engage actively rather than passively; come to office hours to get help, meet other scholars, and get to know your facilitator; and take responsibility for your own pacing and progress. About this syllabus. This is the plan for the On-Demand (asynchronous) section of the course as designed. It is a full-year course; you pace through the four quarters of your enrolled year. Optima also offers this course as a Live section with the same content and expectations, described in its own syllabus. Exact pacing and a few activities may vary from term to term. Your facilitator will confirm the specifics for your section.

COURSE OVERVIEW

Philosophy Honors: Ethics is a yearlong survey of moral philosophy in the Western tradition, moving from the ancient search for moral knowledge through the major frameworks philosophers have used to answer it. Scholars begin with Plato's Euthyphro and the challenges of moral epistemology, move through utilitarian and Kantian accounts of consequence and duty, study Aristotle's virtue ethics and his account of human flourishing, and close with Aquinas's natural law tradition. Each quarter tests its framework against real objections and hard cases, and the course ends with a capstone essay comparing all four accounts of morality against one another.

WHAT SCHOLARS WILL LEARN TO DO
  • Distinguish descriptive from normative claims and identify when a genuine ethical question arises.
  • Evaluate the major challenges to moral knowledge: emotivism, moral relativism, and the fact/value gap.
  • Compare consequentialist and Kantian accounts of right action, including utilitarianism and the categorical imperative.
  • Explain Aristotle's account of eudaimonia, the virtues, and practical wisdom (phronesis).
  • Apply the doctrine of the mean and the cardinal virtues to specific cases of character.
  • Explain Aquinas's natural law theory, the doctrine of double effect, and the basic human goods.
  • Evaluate applied ethical questions in medicine, war, and emerging technology using multiple frameworks.
  • Construct and defend a reasoned position on which account of morality is most adequate.

The course builds toward a capstone-depth essay at the close of each quarter. Target dates below follow a sample full-year pacing; you pace to your own enrolled term, keeping each milestone roughly in order.

ON-DEMAND (ASYNCHRONOUS) LEARNING

In the On-Demand section you move through the course at your own pace within each quarter, guided by due dates that keep you on track. All assignments for a quarter open at its start and close at its end. Because the course is On-Demand, there is no grade penalty for missing an individual due date; any assignment not completed by the end of the quarter receives a zero, and assignments submitted in the final 14 days of a quarter receive a 10% deduction, so steady pacing matters.

Attendance is measured by assignment completion. Per school policy, a scholar who completes no assignment for ten consecutive school days, without notifying the school of an absence in advance, may be dropped from the course. Completion means a sincere attempt: real effort on real work. Rushed work, wrong or corrupted files, irrelevant or nonsense submissions, AI-generated filler, and word-salad responses do not count.

You are never on your own. A live facilitator grades your work, gives feedback, and hosts a weekly study hall and VR workshops.

This course is also taught as a Live (synchronous) section that meets on a schedule on Optima's VR campus. If that is the section you are enrolled in, use the Live syllabus instead of this one.

USING AI IN THIS COURSE

Optima's AI policy does not ask whether a scholar used AI. It asks whether AI was used honestly, skillfully, and in a way that genuinely built your own thinking. AI may support your work, but it may not do the reasoning an assignment asks of you.

WHICH AI TOOLS YOU MAY USE
  • Every scholar. Any AI used for this course is school-controlled: tools built into Canvas assignments and into Optima's VR platform, set up to ask you questions and prompt your thinking rather than hand you answers. No assignment in this course requires a personal AI account.
  • Scholars under 14. Your facilitator may not ask, suggest, or require that you use an AI tool outside those school-controlled platforms. Your AI work for this course happens in Canvas and in VR.
  • Scholars 14 and older. Whether you use an outside AI tool for schoolwork is your family's decision, not the school's. It requires written parent or guardian permission on file with your facilitator, and your parent or guardian selects the tool, sets up the account, monitors it, and stays responsible for it. Optima does not provide, endorse, or manage personal AI accounts. Your facilitator's part is to judge whether the AI was used well.
WHAT IS EXPECTED WHEN YOU USE AI
  • Document it. Record the tool, the prompt you gave it, and the date. Using AI is not plagiarism. Turning in AI-generated work as entirely your own thought, with no documentation, is.
  • Verify it. AI states wrong things confidently, and you are responsible for every claim you submit, so check it against a credible source before it goes into your work. Verification is one of the skills this course grades.
  • Sound like yourself. Your work should read the way you write and speak in the rest of the course, take a real position rather than hedging, and be something you can explain on the spot, on camera or in VR, when your facilitator asks a follow-up question you did not expect.
  • Keep the process, not just the product. Prompt logs, drafts, revision notes, and VR recordings are gradeable evidence of your thinking. When an assignment asks for them, they count toward your grade.

Some assignments limit or exclude AI so that you build the underlying skill yourself, and the assignment page will say so. The reason is practical: you cannot judge whether an AI's answer is any good unless you can do the work without it.

LEARNING IN VIRTUAL REALITY

Optima is a virtual-reality school. Alongside your Canvas coursework, you will join immersive sessions on Optima's VR campus, where you meet teachers and fellow scholars, take part in live activities, and explore places and ideas you could not visit in an ordinary classroom. Keep your headset charged and ready for any scheduled VR sessions, and treat the VR campus with the same courtesy and seriousness you would a physical one. If you ever cannot get into VR for a session, tell your facilitator: there is an alternative way to take part so you do not fall behind.

BEING AN OPTIMA SCHOLAR

Optima's mission is an excellent, virtue-centered education, and virtue is at the center of this course as much as any other. Every scholar is expected to practice the seven virtues that shape life at Optima: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. In practice that means: do your own honest work; treat everyone you meet in, through, or because of this course with respect, in writing, in discussion, and in VR; engage actively rather than passively; come to office hours to get help, meet other scholars, and get to know your facilitator; and take responsibility for your own pacing and progress. You belong to a house and a community of scholars, not only to a course.

assignments.title: 1.02 · Moral Convergence Across Traditions
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Widely separated civilizations, with no shared history, converge on certain moral demands. This convergence is a philosophical datum: it needs explaining. The lesson examined four ancient moral sources. This assignment asks you to identify a point of convergence among them and evaluate what the convergence shows, or fails to show, about the nature of morality.

Focus Question

Does convergence across radically different cultures point toward a common moral reality, or is there a better explanation?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, complete a comparison chart in your course notebook using the four sources from the lesson: the Code of Hammurabi, Exodus 20, the Analects of Confucius, and Matthew 5–7. For each source, note:

  1. The grounding given for the moral rules it presents
  2. One rule or demand that surprised you

Your Assignment

Write a short analysis of 200–300 words that addresses all three of the following:

  1. Identify one moral demand shared across at least three of the four sources. Be specific: name the demand and the sources that contain it.
  2. Explain what this convergence suggests about the nature of morality. What philosophical conclusion, if any, is it reasonable to draw?
  3. Address the central question: Does the convergence point toward a common moral reality, or is there a better explanation available? State and briefly support your position.

Success Criteria

A strong short analysis will:

  • Name a specific shared demand rather than a vague general claim (e.g., "fairness")
  • Correctly identify the sources that share it
  • Distinguish between what convergence shows and what it merely suggests
  • Take a clear position on the focus question and support it with at least one reason
  • Stay within the word count while addressing all three parts

Submitting Your Work

Submit your short analysis as a typed document to the Assignment 1.02 submission box in Canvas. 200–300 words. You do not need a formal title or header, but your name and the assignment number should appear at the top of the document.

Submission Method Update

assignments.title: 1.03 · The Case Against Emotivism
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Emotivism holds that moral statements are not claims about the world but expressions of the speaker's feelings. A.J. Ayer, its most rigorous defender, argues that moral utterances lack truth value and therefore cannot be the objects of knowledge. The lesson examined this position and identified three serious problems it cannot answer. This assignment asks you to engage the position directly: present it fairly, then evaluate it honestly.

Focus Question

Is emotivism a convincing account of what moral language means? What is the most serious thing it gets wrong?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, read the assigned excerpt from Ayer's Language, Truth and Logic, Chapter 6. In your course notebook:

  1. Write Ayer's core claim in your own words.
  2. Identify the passage where he most clearly distinguishes moral utterances from factual statements.

Your Assignment

Write a short essay of 300–400 words that does the following:

  1. Present the strongest version of the emotivist position. Do not caricature it: explain why a serious philosopher found it compelling.
  2. Identify the most serious weakness of emotivism. Choose one problem from those examined in the lesson and explain why it is genuinely difficult for the emotivist to answer.
  3. Support your evaluation with at least one specific example. The example can be a moral situation, a moral argument, or a kind of moral discourse that emotivism handles poorly.

Success Criteria

A strong short essay will:

  • Present emotivism in a form its defenders would recognize as fair
  • Choose one specific weakness rather than listing several superficially
  • Explain why the weakness is a problem for the theory, not just an inconvenience
  • Use a specific example that makes the weakness concrete
  • Reference Ayer's text accurately at least once

Submitting Your Work

assignments.title: 1.04 · Evaluating Moral Relativism
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Moral relativism holds that moral truth is relative to the culture or individual who holds it: there are no moral facts independent of some social or personal framework. This is one of the most widespread views in contemporary popular culture, and one of the most philosophically vulnerable. The lesson examined its strongest forms and its most serious internal problem. This assignment asks you to engage it as a philosophical position rather than dismiss it reflexively.

Focus Question

Can moral relativism survive philosophical scrutiny, or does it undermine itself the moment it makes any claim on us?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, read the assigned excerpt from Plato's Theaetetus, the Protagoras section. In your course notebook:

  1. Find the passage where Socrates presents the self-refutation of Protagoras' doctrine.
  2. Paraphrase the argument in two or three sentences in your own words.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 300–400 words that addresses all three of the following:

  1. Present the strongest form of moral relativism. What does it claim, and why might a thoughtful person find it appealing? Do not misrepresent the position in order to make it easier to criticize.
  2. Explain the self-refutation problem. Using Plato's Theaetetus as your reference, explain how the strongest form of relativism appears to undermine itself.
  3. Address whether the relativist has a response available. Can the self-refutation problem be answered? State your position and support it with at least one reason.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Present relativism in its strongest form rather than a simplified version
  • Explain the self-refutation problem accurately, with specific reference to the Theaetetus
  • Take a clear position on whether the relativist can respond
  • Support that position with at least one specific reason
  • Avoid the common error of claiming the issue is "just a matter of opinion"

Submitting Your Work

assignments.title: 1.05 · Can Morality Be Rationally Grounded?
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Hume observed that no argument can move validly from purely descriptive premises ("what is") to normative conclusions ("what ought to be"). This gap between fact and value is one of the most discussed problems in modern ethics. The lesson examined three responses. This assignment asks you to evaluate the central claim that the is/ought gap makes rational grounding for ethics impossible, and to defend the response you find most convincing.

Focus Question

Does Hume's is/ought observation show that ethics cannot be rationally grounded? Or is there a way to move from facts about human nature or reason to moral conclusions?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, read the assigned excerpt from Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil, Preface and Sections 1–6. In your course notebook:

  1. Identify Nietzsche's main target of criticism.
  2. Write one sentence on what he means by "dogmatic philosophy" in ethics.
  3. Note whether Nietzsche's critique applies to Socratic questioning or only to uncritical moral tradition.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 350–450 words that does the following:

  1. State the argument from the is/ought gap in its strongest form. Explain precisely what the problem is: what kind of move does it forbid, and why?
  2. Present and evaluate the three responses examined in the lesson. You do not need to treat each one at length: a sentence or two on each is enough to show that you understand them.
  3. Defend your position on which response is most convincing. State your position clearly and give at least one reason in its favor. Use Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil to support your analysis.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • State the is/ought argument precisely, not vaguely
  • Correctly characterize all three responses from the lesson
  • Defend a position with at least one specific reason
  • Accurately reference Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil
  • Show philosophical reasoning, not just assertion

This module examined three serious challenges to the idea that ethics can be a domain of genuine knowledge: emotivism (moral claims express feelings rather than facts), moral relativism (moral truth is relative to culture, with no standard above any particular culture's code), and the joint challenge from Hume's gap between "is" and "ought" and Nietzsche's critique of inherited moral tradition. Each challenge, if it succeeded, would mean something different about whether ethical inquiry is even possible.

Focus Question

Which of the three obstacles examined this module poses the most serious threat to the possibility of moral knowledge, and does it actually succeed?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, review your notes from all three weeks of this module:

  1. Lesson 1.03: Ayer's emotivism and the problems it faces, including the Frege-Geach problem.
  2. Lesson 1.04: Protagoras and moral relativism, including the self-refutation and tolerance objections.
  3. Lesson 1.05: Hume's is-ought gap and Nietzsche's challenge to moral tradition.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 500–700 words that does the following:

  1. Restate all three obstacles accurately, in your own words: emotivism, moral relativism, and the Humean/Nietzschean challenge.
  2. Identify which one poses the most serious threat to moral knowledge, and explain why it is a bigger problem than the other two.
  3. Evaluate whether your chosen obstacle actually succeeds. Does it fully defeat the possibility of moral knowledge, or does it fail for some specific, identifiable reason?
  4. Address the strongest objection to your evaluation and explain how you respond to it.

Success Criteria

A strong capstone essay will:

  • Represent all three obstacles accurately and fairly
  • Make a clear comparative judgment about which is most serious, with real reasons
  • Take and defend a specific position on whether the chosen obstacle succeeds
  • Engage a genuine objection rather than a weak one

assignments.title: 1.06 · What Does Moral Sentimentalism Explain?
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Moral sentimentalism, associated especially with Hume and later Francis Hutcheson, grounds moral judgment in human feeling rather than in reason or God's commands. The lesson examined what this approach illuminates about our actual moral psychology and identified three serious problems it struggles to resolve. This assignment asks you to assess the theory's explanatory reach: what it gets right, and where it falls short.

Focus Question

What does moral sentimentalism genuinely explain about moral life, and what does it fail to account for?

Primary Source Preparation

  1. Identify Hume's account of what moral sentiment is.
  2. Note the passage where he acknowledges the need for an impartial standpoint to correct natural partiality.

Your Assignment

Write a short essay of 250–350 words that does the following:

  1. Identify what moral sentimentalism gets right. What does grounding morality in feeling capture about moral experience that purely rationalist accounts miss?
  2. Identify what moral sentimentalism fails to account for. Choose one of the three problems discussed in the lesson and explain why it is genuinely difficult for sentimentalism to resolve.
  3. Reference Hume's Enquiry at least once in support of your analysis.

  • Identify a specific strength, not a general one ("it captures something real")
  • Choose one specific problem from the lesson, not multiple problems treated vaguely

assignments.title: 1.07 · What Evolution Can and Cannot Explain
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Darwin's account of the moral instincts showed that moral feelings have an evolutionary history and a biological function. This is a significant scientific contribution. But the lesson established a crucial limit: explaining how moral instincts arose is not the same as justifying them. A behavior that evolved because it aided survival is not thereby shown to be morally good. This assignment asks you to articulate that distinction and evaluate its significance.

Focus Question

What does evolutionary ethics illuminate about moral life, and what fundamental philosophical question does it leave unanswered?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, read the assigned excerpt from Darwin's The Descent of Man, Chapter 4. In your course notebook:

  1. Identify which traits Darwin thinks evolved and explain the evolutionary reason he gives.
  2. Note whether Darwin himself claims these traits are morally justified or merely psychologically real.

Your Assignment

Write a short analysis of 250–350 words that addresses the following:

  1. Explain what evolutionary ethics contributes to our understanding of moral life. What genuine insight does it provide that a purely abstract philosophical account of morality would miss?
  2. Identify the philosophical question it leaves unanswered. State the question precisely, and explain why evolutionary evidence alone cannot answer it.
  3. Reference Darwin's Descent of Man to support your analysis.

Success Criteria

A strong short analysis will:

  • Name a specific insight that evolutionary ethics provides, not a vague one
  • State the unanswered philosophical question precisely: what kind of question is it, and why does science not answer it?
  • Make the distinction between descriptive (evolutionary) and normative (philosophical) claims explicit
  • Reference Darwin's text accurately

assignments.title: 1.08 · What the Scientific Approaches to Ethics Achieve
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This module examined three scientific approaches to moral life: moral sentimentalism, evolutionary ethics, and moral psychology (including neuroscience). Each offers genuine insight into the psychological and biological mechanisms behind moral judgment. Each also runs into the same fundamental limit. This assignment is a synthesis reflection: looking across all three approaches, you will identify what they collectively illuminate and what question they consistently leave open.

Focus Question

Across sentimentalism, evolutionary ethics, and moral psychology, what does the scientific approach illuminate about moral life, and what question does it consistently fail to answer?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, read the assigned excerpt from Jonathan Haidt, "The Emotional Dog and Its Rational Tail" (Psychological Review, 2001). In your course notebook:

  1. Identify Haidt's core claim and the main piece of evidence he uses to support it.
  2. Write one paragraph in response: does showing that moral reasoning often rationalizes intuition show that moral reasoning is unreliable?

Your Assignment

Write a Module 3 reflection of 300–400 words that addresses the following:

  1. What the scientific approaches illuminate. Across moral sentimentalism, evolutionary ethics, and moral psychology, identify one thing each approach illuminates about moral life that a purely abstract philosophical account would miss. You may treat them briefly, but each should appear.
  2. What they consistently fail to answer. Identify the one philosophical question that all three approaches share the same inability to answer. State the question precisely, not vaguely.
  3. Reference Haidt's "Emotional Dog" paper somewhere in your analysis.

Success Criteria

A strong Module 3 reflection will:

  • Address all three approaches, not just one or two
  • Identify a shared limitation, not three separate limitations

assignments.title: Module 3 Capstone: What Can Science Tell Us About Morality?
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This module examined three scientific approaches to morality: moral sense theory (Hutcheson and Hume's account of natural sympathy), evolutionary ethics (Darwin's account of the origin of social instincts), and moral psychology (Haidt's research on moral intuition and Damasio's patients). Each approach tries to explain something real about how moral judgment works. None of them, on its own, settles whether morality is more than a natural phenomenon.

Across moral sense theory, evolutionary ethics, and moral psychology, what has the scientific study of morality actually established, and what has it failed to establish?

  2. Identify one limitation all three approaches share. Consider the origin/justification distinction, the naturalistic fallacy, or the gap between what a science of morality can describe and what it can normatively justify.
  3. Take a position: does the scientific evidence examined this module strengthen or weaken confidence in ethics as a domain of genuine knowledge, and why?
  4. Address the strongest objection to your position.

assignments.title: 2.04 · The Justice Objection to Utilitarianism
assignments.html:
Content Focus

The justice objection to utilitarianism holds that the theory can, in principle, justify punishing an innocent person, breaking a promise, or violating a right whenever doing so produces greater aggregate welfare. This objection cuts deep: it charges that utilitarianism treats justice as merely instrumental, as something to be calculated rather than respected. Mill was aware of this objection and attempted to accommodate justice within the utilitarian framework. This assignment asks you to examine that attempt.

Focus Question

Can utilitarianism accommodate justice, or does treating justice as a means rather than an end undermine it as a moral theory?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, read John Stuart Mill's Utilitarianism, Chapters 3 and 5. In your course notebook, note how Mill tries to accommodate justice within the utilitarian framework. Pay particular attention to Chapter 5, where Mill argues that justice is the most vital part of morality because it corresponds to the most urgent social utilities.

Your Assignment

Write an essay draft of 400–500 words that does the following:

  1. Present the strongest form of the justice objection to utilitarianism. Include at least one specific example that makes the objection vivid: a case where utilitarianism seems to require something that strikes most people as deeply unjust.
  2. Construct the best utilitarian response you can. Use Mill's argument from Chapter 5 and any other resources available from within the utilitarian tradition. The response should be genuinely strong, not a straw man.

This is a draft. You will have the opportunity to revise it for clarity and argument strength before the end of the quarter.

Success Criteria

A strong draft will:

  • Present the justice objection in its strongest form, not a weak version
  • Use a specific example to make the objection concrete
  • Construct a utilitarian response that draws on Mill's own argument
  • Leave the reader with a clear sense of whether the response succeeds
  • Reference Mill's Utilitarianism Chapters 3 and 5 accurately

assignments.html:
Content Focus

Kant argues that morality is grounded in reason alone. The categorical imperative has two main formulations: act only on a maxim you could will to become a universal law, and always treat rational beings as ends in themselves, never merely as means.

Focus Question

Pick one of Kant's own examples and apply one formulation of the categorical imperative to it. What verdict does it deliver?

Your Warm-Up

Write a short response of 150–250 words that does the following:

  1. Choose one example: the honest shopkeeper, the person contemplating suicide, or the person making a false promise.
  2. Apply one formulation of the categorical imperative (universalizability or humanity) to it, and state what verdict it delivers.
  3. Say whether the verdict seems right to you, in one or two sentences.

Success Criteria

This is a warm-up, not a full essay. A complete response applies one formulation correctly to one example and gives a real reaction to the verdict.

Submitting Your Work

assignments.title: 2.06 · The Case For or Against Kantian Deontology
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Kantian deontology grounds morality in the dignity of rational beings and the unconditional nature of moral law. Its great strength is its insistence that persons must never be treated as mere means. Its vulnerabilities appear in hard cases: what should be said to the murderer at the door who asks where your friend is hiding? And what happens when two genuine duties conflict? This assignment asks you to take a position and defend it, engaging at least one of these objections directly.

Focus Question

Is Kantian deontology an adequate moral theory? Does its account of human dignity withstand its most serious objections?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, read the assigned excerpts:

  1. Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Section 3
  2. Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Articles 1, 4, and 5

In your notebook, note how the language of dignity appears in each UDHR article and how it connects to Kant's account of rational beings as ends in themselves.

Your Assignment

Write an essay draft of 400–500 words that does the following:

  1. Take a position: argue either for or against the adequacy of Kantian deontology as a moral theory.
  2. Address at least one of the two objections discussed in the lesson: the lying murderer case or the problem of conflicting duties. Present the strongest version of the objection and the strongest response available from within the Kantian tradition.
  3. Reference both the Groundwork and the Universal Declaration in your argument.

This is a draft. You will have the opportunity to revise it before the end of the quarter.

Success Criteria

A strong draft will:

  • State and defend a clear position on Kantian deontology
  • Present one objection in its strongest form
  • Present the strongest Kantian response to that objection
  • Reference both the Groundwork and the Universal Declaration accurately
  • Maintain a philosophical rather than merely rhetorical tone

Submitting Your Work

assignments.title: 2.09 · Consequentialism and Deontology: A Case Study Comparison
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Quarter 2 examined consequentialism and Kantian deontology as the two dominant frameworks in modern ethics. Both theories are rigorous, systematic, and capable of illuminating moral situations. Both also have characteristic blind spots. The Quarter 2 synthesis essay asks you to put both frameworks to work on a single case, identify where they agree and where they diverge, and evaluate which provides the more compelling analysis. This is the central philosophical exercise of the quarter: not describing theories but using them.

Focus Question

When consequentialism and Kantian deontology are applied to the same case, where do they agree, where do they diverge, and which framework provides the more compelling moral analysis?

Primary Sources Required

Your essay must make accurate reference to at least two of the following primary sources from Quarter 2:

  • Mill, Utilitarianism
  • Bentham, Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
  • Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
  • Rawls, A Theory of Justice

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 700–900 words that does the following:

  1. Choose a case study. It can be historical (such as the Hiroshima decision from Lesson 2.01), a moral dilemma from the applied ethics lesson, or a case of your own choosing. State the case clearly at the outset.
  2. Apply both frameworks to the case. Show what verdict each reaches and how it arrives there. Be precise about each framework's reasoning, not just its conclusion.
  3. Identify the key point of disagreement between the frameworks. If they agree on the verdict but disagree on the reason, that disagreement is also worth examining.
  4. Evaluate which framework provides the more compelling moral analysis. Defend your evaluation with reasons. Do not simply declare a winner: explain what makes one framework's reasoning stronger in this case.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Choose a case with genuine moral complexity, not a trivial or one-sided example
  • Apply both frameworks precisely, not as caricatures
  • Identify the key disagreement with specificity
  • Defend a verdict on which framework is more compelling with at least two reasons

assignments.title: Module 4 Capstone: Beyond Consequentialism and Deontology
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This module examined how twentieth-century moral philosophy moved beyond strict consequentialism and deontology: the Belmont Report's applied-ethics tradition, Ross's prima facie duties and Rawls's justice as fairness as alternatives to universal principles, and Anscombe's challenge to the entire modern framework. Anscombe's challenge is where Quarter 2 ends and where Quarter 3's turn to virtue ethics begins.

Focus Question

Having studied Ross's prima facie duties, Rawlsian justice as fairness, and Anscombe's challenge to modern moral philosophy, is either consequentialism or deontology still the right framework for ethics, or does modern moral philosophy point somewhere else?

  3. Evaluate whether Anscombe's challenge is fair to consequentialism and deontology as you have studied them this semester, or whether it misses something important about either theory.
  4. Having now worked through Quarter 2 in full, state which approach you find most defensible: consequentialist, deontological, or something else that Ross, Rawls, or Anscombe point toward, and why.

Aristotle opens the Nicomachean Ethics with the observation that every human action aims at some good. The highest good is the one we pursue for its own sake, and Aristotle's name for it is eudaimonia, best understood as flourishing or living well.

assignments.title: 3.02 · Does the Function Argument Succeed? (Warm-Up)

Content Focus

Focus Question

Does the function argument succeed? Can ethics be grounded in an account of the human function?

  1. State the argument in your own words, in a few sentences, showing its steps and not only its conclusion.
  2. Say whether you think it succeeds, and give one clear reason.
  3. Name one objection a critic would press against your view.

assignments.title: Q3 Module 1 Capstone: Is Flourishing Grounded in Human Nature?
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This module began with Aristotle's claim in the Nicomachean Ethics that every human action aims at some good, and that the highest good, the one pursued for its own sake, is eudaimonia, flourishing or living well. It then examined the function argument in NE I.7, which holds that to know what is good for humans we must first know what humans are for. Together they make a bold proposal: that an account of the good life can be grounded in an account of human nature.

Focus Question

Does Aristotle's account of the highest good, supported by the function argument, succeed in grounding the good life in human nature?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, review your notes from every lesson in this module:

  1. Lesson 3.01: the highest good and Aristotle's formal requirements for it (NE I.1–5).
  2. Lesson 3.02: the function argument and how Aristotle rules out mere life and sentient life before arriving at rational activity in accordance with excellence (NE I.7).

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 500–700 words that does the following:

  1. Explain how the two parts fit together. State Aristotle's account of the highest good and the function argument accurately, and show how the second is meant to support the first.
  2. Test them on a concrete case. Describe a life you would call genuinely flourishing, and show whether Aristotle's account explains why it flourishes.
  3. Evaluate the function argument. Take a clear position on whether it succeeds in grounding ethics in human nature, and give your reasons.
  4. Address the strongest objection to your own evaluation and explain how you respond to it.

Success Criteria

A strong capstone essay will:

  • A specific life is described and tested against Aristotle's account, with honest attention to where the fit is imperfect

assignments.title: 3.03 · A Portrait of Practical Wisdom (Warm-Up)
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Practical wisdom, or phronesis, is the capacity to see what a situation requires, deliberate well, and act accordingly. Aristotle sets it apart from technical skill (techne): a craftsman can follow a formula, but a practically wise person must respond to what no formula captures (NE VI.4–7).

Focus Question

What does practical wisdom look like in practice, and what does it do that rule-following cannot?

  2. Explain what they saw in the situation that a rule would have missed or gotten wrong.
  3. Say why this is practical wisdom and not simply cleverness.

assignments.title: Q3 Module 2 Capstone: Practical Wisdom and Responsibility for Character
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This module examined two parts of Aristotle's account of how virtue comes to be. Virtues of character are formed through habit: we become just by doing just things. But habit alone does not complete virtue. Practical wisdom, phronesis, is the capacity to see what a situation requires, and Aristotle sets it apart from technical skill and from mere natural tendency. From these claims Aristotle draws a demanding conclusion: that we are responsible for our characters.

Focus Question

How do habituation and practical wisdom together produce virtue, and does Aristotle succeed in showing that we are responsible for the characters they produce?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, review your notes from every lesson in this module:

  1. Lesson 3.03: practical wisdom, its contrast with technical skill, and Aristotle's argument that natural virtue is not yet virtue (NE VI.4–7 and 12–13).
  2. Lesson 3.04: habituation, the difference between acting virtuously and having the virtue, and the question of responsibility for character (NE II.1–4).

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 500–700 words that does the following:

  1. Explain both parts accurately. State what habituation does and what practical wisdom adds, in your own words and with reference to the text.
  2. Show how they relate. Explain why, on Aristotle's view, neither one is sufficient for virtue by itself.
  3. Evaluate Aristotle's claim that we are responsible for our characters. Take a clear position on whether his account is fair, and give your reasons.
  4. Address the strongest objection to your own evaluation and explain how you respond to it.

Success Criteria

A strong capstone essay will:

  • Each is stated accurately and in the student's own words, with accurate reference to the text
  • Explains clearly why neither habituation nor practical wisdom is sufficient for virtue by itself
  • Takes a clear, well-reasoned position on whether Aristotle's account of responsibility for character is fair
  • Engages a genuine, serious objection to the essay's own evaluation and responds to it

  2. Name its domain, the vice of deficiency, and the vice of excess.
  3. Explain in a sentence or two why the mean differs from one person or situation to another, using one concrete example.

assignments.title: 3.06 · A Cardinal Virtue in Contemporary Life
assignments.html:
Content Focus

The four cardinal virtues, courage, temperance, justice, and prudence, are not abstract ideals but dispositions that manifest in specific ways in specific lives. Plato introduced them in the Republic as the virtues that constitute a well-ordered soul and a well-ordered city. Aristotle developed each in detail in the Nicomachean Ethics, and Aquinas integrated them into a natural law framework. This assignment asks you to make one of these virtues concrete by developing a sustained contemporary example.

Focus Question

What does one cardinal virtue look like when it is fully developed in a contemporary person? What does its opposing vice look like, and what is needed to cultivate the virtue?

Primary Sources

Draw on at least one of the following in your essay:

  • Plato, Republic, Book IV (the analysis of the cardinal virtues)
  • Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Books III–IV (the individual virtues)
  • Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II (the cardinal virtues)

Your Assignment

Write a short essay of 300–400 words that does all of the following:

  1. Choose one cardinal virtue: courage, temperance, justice, or prudence.
  2. Describe what a fully developed example of this virtue looks like in contemporary life. Be specific: describe the person's character, the situations where the virtue appears, and what distinguishes the virtuous response from the vicious one.
  3. Describe what the opposing vice looks like. Show how someone with a deficient or excessive version of this disposition would act differently.
  4. Explain what is needed to develop the virtue. What habits, practices, or conditions produce it?

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Develop a sustained, specific contemporary example rather than an abstract description
  • Describe both the virtue and its opposing vice with equal specificity
  • Connect the example to the classical account in at least one primary source
  • Address what is needed to develop the virtue, not just what it looks like

Socrates denied that akrasia (acting against one's better judgment) is possible: if you truly know what is good, you will pursue it. What appears to be weakness of will is, on his account, really a form of ignorance. Aristotle took this view head-on in NE Book VII and argued that Socrates is simply wrong: people do sometimes act against their better judgment, and the explanation does not require denying that they knew what was right. This is one of the most direct disagreements in the history of ethics. This assignment asks you to evaluate it.

Focus Question

Who has the better account of moral failure: Socrates or Aristotle? Is akrasia possible, and what does your answer imply about moral responsibility?

Primary Source

Draw on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, Book VII, Chapters 1–3, where Aristotle presents and responds to the Socratic denial of akrasia. You may also reference Socrates' position as it appears in Plato's Protagoras.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 350–450 words that does the following:

  1. State both positions with precision: the Socratic denial of akrasia and Aristotle's account of weakness of will as a real phenomenon.
  2. Defend your position on which account is more adequate. State clearly whether you side with Socrates or Aristotle and give at least two reasons for your verdict.
  3. Address one serious difficulty with the view you have defended. What is the strongest objection to it, and how would you respond?

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • State both positions accurately and fairly
  • Take a clear, defended position with at least two reasons
  • Identify a genuine difficulty with the defended view

assignments.title: 3.09 · Eudaimonia and Virtue: Aristotle's Central Claim
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Aristotle's central claim in the Nicomachean Ethics is that eudaimonia is the highest good and that virtue is not merely a means to it but its constitutive element: to live virtuously is, in the most important sense, to flourish. This claim holds together the entire architecture of virtue ethics and sets it apart from both consequentialism and Kantian deontology. The Quarter 3 synthesis essay asks you to explain this claim, evaluate its most compelling evidence, and identify and respond to its most serious objection.

Focus Question

What does Aristotle mean when he claims that eudaimonia is the highest good and that virtue is its constitutive element? What is the strongest evidence for this claim, and what is the most serious objection to it?

Primary Sources Required

Your essay must make accurate reference to at least two primary sources from Quarter 3. Recommended options:

  • Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I (highest good, function argument)
  • Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II (character, habituation, virtue)
  • Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VI (phronesis)
  • Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Books VIII–IX (friendship)
  • Plato, Republic, Book IV (cardinal virtues)

Your Assignment

Write a synthesis essay of 600–800 words that does the following:

  1. Explain Aristotle's central claim. What does it mean to say that eudaimonia is the highest good and that virtue is its constitutive element rather than merely its means? Make clear why this claim is philosophically significant.
  2. Identify its strongest evidence. What argument or consideration from the course do you find most compelling in its support? Draw on specific primary source material.
  3. Identify and respond to the most serious objection. What is the strongest challenge to Aristotle's claim? State it fairly and provide the best response you can construct.

Success Criteria

A strong synthesis essay will:

  • Explain Aristotle's claim with philosophical precision, not just paraphrase
  • Identify what makes virtue constitutive rather than merely instrumental
  • Select evidence that genuinely supports the claim, with specific primary source reference
  • State the objection fairly enough that a critic would recognize it
  • Construct a response to the objection that engages it directly

assignments.title: Q3 Module 3 Capstone: How Virtue Is Lived, Sustained, and Lost
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This module followed Aristotle's account of virtue from its definition to its practice. Virtue is a disposition to choose the mean between an excess and a deficiency, and the cardinal virtues (courage, temperance, justice, and prudence) give that account its concrete content. Aristotle also holds that no one lives well without friends, since the virtuous friend is "another self" through whom we exercise our virtues and come to know ourselves. And he takes up a hard question that divides him from Socrates: whether a person can know what is good and still fail to do it.

Focus Question

What does Aristotle's account say about how virtue is expressed, sustained, and lost, and does it explain moral failure as well as it explains moral success?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, review your notes from every lesson in this module:

  1. Lessons 3.05 and 3.06: the doctrine of the mean (NE II.5–9) and the cardinal virtues, with Plato's Republic IV and Aristotle's NE III–IV.
  2. Lesson 3.07: friendship and the good life, especially the claim that the virtuous friend is "another self" (NE VIII–IX).
  3. Lesson 3.08: the Socratic denial of weakness of will and Aristotle's reply (NE VII.1–3).

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 500–700 words that does the following:

  1. Explain how virtue shows up in action. Use the doctrine of the mean and at least one cardinal virtue, with its vices of excess and deficiency, to show what virtuous action looks like.
  2. Explain what sustains virtue. Show what Aristotle's account of friendship adds to the picture of how a person comes to live virtuously and continues to do so.
  3. Evaluate Aristotle's account of moral failure. State the Socratic denial of weakness of will and Aristotle's reply, and take a clear position on whether Aristotle explains failure as well as he explains success.
  4. Address the strongest objection to your own evaluation and explain how you respond to it.

Success Criteria

A strong capstone essay will:

  • The doctrine of the mean and at least one cardinal virtue are explained accurately, with its excess and deficiency named
  • Explains clearly what friendship adds to the formation and exercise of virtue, with accurate reference to Aristotle
  • States the Socratic and Aristotelian positions accurately and takes a clear, well-reasoned position on whether Aristotle explains failure as well as success
  • Engages a genuine, serious objection to the essay's own evaluation and responds to it

assignments.title: 4.01 · Natural Law and Human Law: Drawing the Distinction
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Natural law theory holds that there is a moral order written into the structure of reality, discoverable by human reason, that stands above and judges human-made law. Aquinas developed the most systematic account of this tradition, distinguishing four tiers of law: eternal, divine, natural, and human. The key claim is that human laws which violate natural law are not genuine laws at all but corruptions of law. This distinction is not merely theoretical: it has been invoked in some of the most consequential moral and legal arguments in history.

Focus Question

What is the difference between natural law and human law in Aquinas's framework? Can you identify a historical case where human law violated natural law?

Primary Sources

Draw on Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, Questions 90–94, especially his definitions of law, the hierarchy of law types, and the conditions under which a human law fails to bind in conscience. You may also reference Cicero's De Re Publica for the classical statement of natural law.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 300–400 words that does the following:

  1. Explain the distinction between natural law and human law in Aquinas's framework. What makes each kind of law what it is? What is the relationship between them?
  2. Identify and discuss a historical example in which human law appears to have violated natural law. Explain what natural law the human law violated, and note what the consequence was.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Explain the Aquinas hierarchy accurately, not vaguely
  • State what makes a human law binding and what makes it not binding in conscience
  • Choose a historical example with genuine moral weight, not a trivial one
  • Reference Aquinas's Summa Theologiae accurately

assignments.title: 4.02 · Responding to the Objection About Desire
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Aquinas states the first principle of natural law in a single Latin phrase: bonum est faciendum et prosequendum, et malum vitandum (good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided). This principle rests on the claim that good is what all things seek. It draws on Aristotle's teleology and gives the natural law tradition its fundamental orientation. But the principle faces an immediate objection from anyone who notices how much of what human beings actually seek is harmful or self-destructive. This assignment asks you to develop Aquinas's response.

Focus Question

If "good is what all things seek," but people often seek harmful things, how does Aquinas avoid the conclusion that whatever is sought is therefore good?

Primary Source

Draw on Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, Q94, A2, where Aquinas states and develops the first principle of natural law, including his account of natural inclinations and the relationship between good and being.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 300–400 words that presents and evaluates the following objection and response:

"Aquinas says that 'good is what all things seek.' But people seek all kinds of things, including harmful things. Doesn't this make everything good, or at least everything sought good?"

  1. State the objection fairly. Why is it a genuine challenge to Aquinas's first principle, not merely a misunderstanding?
  2. Construct Aquinas's response. Draw specifically on his account in ST I-II, Q94, A2 to show how he distinguishes genuine goods from apparent goods and how this responds to the objection.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • State the objection precisely enough that it is a real challenge
  • Draw on Aquinas's actual account in Q94, A2, not a paraphrase of the paraphrase
  • Explain the genuine goods/apparent goods distinction clearly
  • Evaluate whether the response is convincing

assignments.title: Q4 Module 1 Capstone: Can Natural Law Judge Human Law?
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This module introduced natural law theory: the claim that there is a moral order discoverable by human reason that stands above and judges human-made law. Aquinas sorted law into four tiers (eternal, divine, natural, and human), held that a human law which violates natural law is a corruption of law, and grounded the whole structure in a first principle: good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided. That principle rests on the claim that good is what all things seek, and it faces an immediate objection from the fact that people often seek harmful things.

Focus Question

Does Aquinas's first principle of natural law give a sound basis for judging human law, once the objection from desire has been answered?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, review your notes from every lesson in this module:

  1. Lesson 4.01: the four tiers of law and the conditions under which a human law fails to bind in conscience (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, Questions 90–94, with Cicero's De Re Publica for the classical statement).
  2. Lesson 4.02: the first principle of natural law, the objection from desire, and Aquinas's distinction between genuine and apparent goods (ST I-II, Q94, A2).

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 500–700 words that does the following:

  1. Restate the framework accurately. Explain the four tiers of law and what makes a human law binding or not binding in conscience.
  2. Explain the first principle and the objection to it. State the objection from desire fairly, and give Aquinas's response using the distinction between genuine and apparent goods.
  3. Evaluate whether the first principle supports judging human law. Take a clear position on whether it gives a sound basis for saying that an unjust human law is not a genuine law.
  4. Address the strongest objection to your own evaluation and explain how you respond to it.

Success Criteria

  • The objection is stated fairly and Aquinas's genuine versus apparent goods response is explained accurately from the text

assignments.title: 4.03 · Are the Basic Goods Incommensurable?
assignments.html:
Content Focus

John Finnis, in the modern natural law tradition, argues that there are seven basic human goods (life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness, and religion) that are self-evident, irreducible, and incommensurable: none can be traded off against another on a common scale of value. This claim has major consequences. If the basic goods are truly incommensurable, then consequentialist aggregation fails: you cannot compensate for the loss of one basic good by increasing another. This assignment asks you to evaluate the incommensurability claim.

Focus Question

Are the basic goods truly incommensurable? Can we ever rationally trade off one basic good against another, or does incommensurability hold?

Primary Source

Draw on Finnis's account of the basic goods and their incommensurability as covered in the lesson. Reference the specific basic goods by name when relevant to your argument.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 300–400 words that takes and defends a position on the incommensurability of the basic goods. Your essay must:

  1. State your position clearly. Do you think the basic goods are incommensurable? Or can they be rationally traded off?
  2. Give at least two reasons in support of your position. Each reason should reference the specific basic goods account rather than abstract philosophical claims alone.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Take a clear position, not a hedged one
  • Give two reasons that reference the basic goods specifically
  • Engage with the strongest objection to the chosen position
  • Show understanding of what incommensurability means and why it matters for ethics

assignments.title: 4.04 · The Case Against Absolute Prohibitions
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Natural law theory holds that some moral prohibitions are absolute: there are actions (such as torturing the innocent, murdering the just, or acting against the basic human goods) that cannot be justified by any consequence, however desirable. Because the basic goods are incommensurable, no calculation can trade the violation of one good for gains in another. This view is demanding and faces a powerful objection: surely there are extreme cases where an absolute prohibition causes more harm than violating it would. This assignment asks you to engage that objection directly.

Focus Question

Are absolute moral prohibitions defensible? Or is there always a conceivable extreme case that shows they must yield to consequences?

Primary Sources

Draw on Aquinas's account of obligation and the natural law framework, and on Finnis's four key requirements of practical reasonableness covered in the lesson. These give you the natural law resources to construct a defense of absolute prohibitions.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 350–450 words that does the following:

  1. Identify the strongest objection to absolute moral prohibitions. State it precisely: what kind of case does it invoke, and what does it claim the objection shows?
  2. Explain how a natural law theorist would respond. Draw on Aquinas's framework and/or Finnis's requirements of practical reasonableness. The response should engage the objection directly rather than simply reasserting the prohibition.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Present the objection in a genuinely challenging form
  • Construct the natural law response using the framework from the lesson
  • Engage the objection rather than reasserting the prohibition without argument
  • Reference Aquinas's account and/or Finnis's requirements accurately
  • Take a clear position on whether the response succeeds

assignments.title: 4.05 · Applying the Doctrine of Double Effect to Hiroshima
assignments.html:
Content Focus

The Doctrine of Double Effect (DDE) is a framework for evaluating actions that have both a good intended effect and a bad foreseen effect. Natural law theory uses it to navigate cases where the absolute prohibition on intentional harm might otherwise seem to conflict with doing good. The lesson presented the DDE's four conditions. This assignment returns to the case introduced in Lesson 2.01: the decision to use atomic weapons against Hiroshima. Here the task is not to argue for or against a framework but to apply a specific tool and follow the argument wherever it leads.

Focus Question

Does the bombing of Hiroshima satisfy all four conditions of the Doctrine of Double Effect? Which conditions, if any, does it fail, and why?

The Four Conditions (for reference)

  1. Nature of the act: The act itself must not be intrinsically evil.
  2. Intention: The agent must intend only the good effect, not the bad effect (even if the bad effect is foreseen).
  3. Causal priority: The bad effect must not be the means by which the good effect is achieved.
  4. Proportionate reason: There must be a sufficiently serious reason for permitting the bad effect to occur.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 400–500 words that applies all four conditions of the DDE to the Hiroshima case. For each condition:

  1. State the condition precisely.
  2. Apply it to the case. Does the bombing satisfy the condition? Explain your reasoning.
  3. Reach a verdict. After evaluating all four conditions, state whether the bombing satisfies the DDE as a whole and what that verdict implies about the morality of the decision.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Apply all four conditions explicitly and in order
  • Engage the most contested conditions (especially intention and causal priority) with care
  • Reach a clear overall verdict, not a hedged one
  • Maintain a philosophical register, not a political one
  • Connect the analysis to the natural law framework for which the DDE was developed

assignments.title: 4.06 · Does Aquinas Escape the Euthyphro Dilemma?
assignments.html:
Content Focus

The Euthyphro dilemma, first raised in Plato's dialogue of that name, poses a fundamental challenge to any view that grounds morality in God's commands: Is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? Each horn is problematic. Aquinas claimed to escape both horns by grounding moral goodness not in arbitrary divine will but in God's rational nature, which is identical with the good itself. This assignment asks you to evaluate whether the escape succeeds.

Focus Question

Does Aquinas's appeal to God's rational nature successfully escape the Euthyphro dilemma? If not, what is the most serious problem that remains?

Primary Sources

Draw on Plato's Euthyphro (for the original dilemma) and Aquinas's account as covered in the lesson. You may also reference Finnis's secular natural law formulation if relevant to your argument.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 350–450 words that does the following:

  1. Explain Aquinas's escape from the Euthyphro dilemma. State both horns of the dilemma and show how Aquinas's position avoids each.
  2. Evaluate whether the escape succeeds. Take a clear position: does Aquinas's resolution fully answer the dilemma?
  3. If you think the escape does not fully succeed, identify the most serious remaining problem and explain what further argument would be needed to address it.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Explain both horns of the Euthyphro dilemma accurately
  • State Aquinas's resolution clearly and show how it avoids each horn
  • Take a clear, defended position on whether the resolution succeeds
  • If arguing it fails, identify a specific remaining problem with precision

assignments.title: 4.07 · Aquinas on Conscience vs. the Mere Feelings Account
assignments.html:
Content Focus

A common contemporary view holds that conscience is just a name for whatever moral feelings we happen to have, shaped by culture, upbringing, and emotion. On this view, when someone says "my conscience tells me X is wrong," they are really saying "I have a strong negative feeling about X." Aquinas developed a very different account: synderesis (the infallible grasp of first moral principles) and conscientia (the fallible application of those principles to cases). These are not feelings but rational capacities. This assignment asks you to show what Aquinas's account can explain that the mere feelings view cannot.

Focus Question

What can Aquinas's account of synderesis and conscientia explain about moral knowledge that a "conscience is mere feeling" account cannot?

Primary Source

Draw on Aquinas's account of synderesis and conscientia as covered in the lesson, including the distinction between vincible and invincible ignorance and Aquinas's claim that erroneous conscience still binds.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 300–400 words that does the following:

  1. State the "mere feelings" view of conscience clearly and fairly. What does it claim, and why might a contemporary person find it plausible?
  2. Explain what is wrong with it, using Aquinas's account of synderesis and conscientia. Show specifically what Aquinas's account can explain that the mere feelings view cannot.
  3. Reference Aquinas's distinctions (synderesis, conscientia, vincible/invincible ignorance) accurately in your argument.

Success Criteria

A strong essay will:

  • Present the mere feelings view fairly enough that its defenders would recognize it
  • Show specifically what the view fails to explain (not just that it is wrong)
  • Use Aquinas's technical distinctions accurately
  • Make a specific positive claim about what Aquinas's account can explain

This module put natural law theory under three tests. The Doctrine of Double Effect gives a four-condition framework for actions with both a good intended effect and a bad foreseen one, and it was applied to the decision at Hiroshima. The Euthyphro dilemma from Plato asks whether something is good because God commands it or whether God commands it because it is good, and Aquinas answers by grounding goodness in God's rational nature. A common contemporary view holds that conscience is just a name for moral feelings, and Aquinas answers with synderesis and conscientia.

Focus Question

Of the three tests examined in this module, which does natural law theory handle least well, and what does that show about the theory?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, review your notes from every lesson in this module:

  1. Lesson 4.05: the four conditions of the Doctrine of Double Effect and their application to the Hiroshima case first met in Lesson 2.01.
  2. Lesson 4.06: the Euthyphro dilemma and Aquinas's appeal to God's rational nature.
  3. Lesson 4.07: synderesis, conscientia, vincible and invincible ignorance, and the contrast with the view that conscience is mere feeling.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 500–700 words that does the following:

  1. Restate all three tests accurately. For each, say what the challenge is and how natural law theory answers it.
  2. Identify the test it handles least well, and explain why that answer is weaker than the other two.
  3. Evaluate what the weakness shows. Take a clear position on whether it damages the theory itself or only one way of formulating it.
  4. Address the strongest objection to your own evaluation and explain how you respond to it.

Success Criteria

A strong capstone essay will:

  • The Doctrine of Double Effect, the Euthyphro dilemma, and the mere-feelings account of conscience are each stated accurately, along with natural law theory's answer to each
  • Identifies which test is handled least well and gives real reasons why that answer is weaker than the other two
  • Takes a clear, well-reasoned position on whether the weakness damages the theory or only one formulation of it
  • Engages a genuine, serious objection to the essay's own evaluation and responds to it

Submitting Your Work

Submission Method

assignments.title: 4.08 · Natural Law Theory: Contribution and Unresolved Objection
assignments.html:
Content Focus

Quarter 4 examined natural law theory from its Aristotelian and Ciceronian roots through Aquinas's synthesis and Finnis's contemporary reconstruction. The theory has been applied to questions of law, conscience, the basic human goods, the Euthyphro dilemma, and the Doctrine of Double Effect. You have now seen what the theory can do. This synthesis essay asks you to assess it: to identify its most important philosophical contribution and to identify the objection it has not yet fully answered.

Focus Question

What is the most important philosophical contribution of natural law theory? What is the most serious objection to it that the tradition has not yet fully resolved?

Primary Sources Required

Your essay must reference at least two primary sources from Quarter 4:

  • Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, QQ 90–94
  • Cicero, De Re Publica (the natural law passage)
  • Finnis, Natural Law and Natural Rights (basic goods and practical reasonableness)
  • Plato, Euthyphro (for the Euthyphro dilemma discussion)

Your Assignment

Write a synthesis essay of 600–800 words that does the following:

  1. Identify natural law theory's most important philosophical contribution. What does it explain or achieve that the other theories examined in this course (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics) do not? Support your claim with specific reference to primary sources.
  2. Identify the most serious unresolved objection. Among the three principal objections examined in the lesson (the is/ought gap, cultural variation, the naturalistic fallacy), which one does natural law theory fail to fully answer? State the objection precisely, explain the best available response, and explain why that response does not fully resolve it.

Success Criteria

A strong synthesis essay will:

  • Make a specific, defensible claim about the theory's contribution rather than a general one
  • Choose the most serious unresolved objection rather than the easiest one to dismiss
  • State the best available response to the objection and explain specifically why it falls short
  • Reference at least two primary sources from the quarter accurately
  • Maintain a tone of genuine philosophical assessment throughout

Submitting Your Work
