assignments.title: 4.09 · The Most Adequate Account of Morality
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This course began with a single question from Plato's Euthyphro: what is the pious thing to do, and how would we know? Over four quarters, you have examined four systematic answers to the deeper question that question opens: consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, and natural law theory. You have read Mill, Kant, Aristotle, and Aquinas. You have applied these frameworks to moral dilemmas, tested them against objections, and followed the arguments wherever they led.

The capstone essay asks you to do what philosophers are ultimately supposed to do: judge. Which of the four theories gives the most adequate account of morality? And what, even in the best account, remains unresolved?

Focus Question

Which of the four ethical theories studied in this course is the most adequate account of morality, and why? What does even the best theory leave unresolved?

Primary Sources Required

Your essay must make specific reference to at least three primary sources from across the course. You may draw from any quarter. Examples include:

  • Plato, Euthyphro or Republic
  • Mill, Utilitarianism
  • Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
  • Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics
  • Aquinas, Summa Theologiae
  • Finnis, Natural Law and Natural Rights
  • Any other primary source read during the course

Your Assignment

Write a capstone essay of 900–1200 words that does the following:

  1. State your thesis. Identify the theory you believe is most adequate and state your central reason in one or two sentences. Be specific: "most adequate" means it best explains the moral facts, best handles the hardest cases, and provides the most coherent account of why morality binds us.
  2. Analyze the competing theories. Engage at least three of the four theories by name. For the theories you do not choose, explain specifically what they fail to account for that your preferred theory handles better. For the theory you choose, explain what it explains well and why its competitors cannot match it.
  3. Address the strongest objection. Identify the most serious objection to your preferred theory and argue for the best available response. If the response does not fully succeed, say so clearly.
  4. State what remains unresolved. Even if your preferred theory is the most adequate, identify one problem it has not fully resolved. What would a philosopher need to show in order to solve it?

Success Criteria

A strong capstone essay will:

  • Defend a specific, argued thesis rather than surveying all four theories neutrally
  • Show genuine comparative analysis: the essay must explain why your theory does better, not just what it claims
  • Reference at least three primary sources accurately and with genuine philosophical engagement
  • Engage the strongest objection rather than an easy one
  • Acknowledge what the best theory still leaves open, without using that acknowledgment to evade the central thesis
  • Maintain a philosophical register throughout: reason-giving, not advocacy

Submitting Your Work

Submit your capstone essay as a typed document to the Assignment 4.09 submission box in Canvas. 900–1200 words. Include your name and the assignment number at the top of the document.

assignments.title: Q4 Module 4 Capstone: One Case, Four Frameworks
assignments.html:
Content Focus

This course has examined four systematic answers to the question of how we ought to act: consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, and natural law theory. A theory shows its quality when it meets a hard case. The decision to use atomic weapons against Hiroshima was first examined in Lesson 2.01 and returned to in Lesson 4.05 through the Doctrine of Double Effect. This capstone asks you to take one case of real moral weight and see what each of the four frameworks makes of it.

Focus Question

When all four frameworks are applied to the same hard case, where do they agree, where do they part ways, and which gives the most illuminating treatment?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing, review your notes from every lesson in this module:

  1. Your notes on the four frameworks from across the course: Mill and Kant (Quarter 2), Aristotle (Quarter 3), and Aquinas and Finnis (Quarter 4).
  2. Lessons 2.01 and 4.05, for the Hiroshima case and the Doctrine of Double Effect, if you choose that case.

Your Assignment

Write an essay of 500–700 words that does the following:

  1. Choose your case. Use the Hiroshima decision, or another real moral case of comparable weight, and state it in a sentence or two.
  2. Apply each of the four frameworks. For each, say what question it puts to the case and what it concludes, in your own words and using the framework's own terms.
  3. Compare and judge. Identify where the frameworks agree, where they disagree, and which gives the most illuminating treatment of this case, with reasons.
  4. Address the strongest objection to your own judgment and explain how you respond to it.

Success Criteria

A strong capstone essay will:

  • Each framework is applied to the case accurately, in its own terms, and without caricature
  • Identifies specifically where the frameworks agree or disagree, and why
  • Takes a clear, well-reasoned position on which framework treats the case best, maintaining a philosophical register rather than a political one
  • Engages a genuine, serious objection to the essay's own judgment and responds to it

Submitting Your Work

Submit your essay as a typed document to the Q4 Module 4 Capstone submission box in Canvas. 500–700 words. Include your name and the module number at the top of the document.

Submission Method

It argues that only Western cultures have ever grasped natural law correctly.

questions.text: According to the lesson, how does Finnis respond to G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy objection?

answers.text: He argues that the basic goods are identified as good because practical reason grasps them as self-evidently valuable, not because they are natural; natural inclinations are a heuristic for attention, not the justification itself.
He concedes that natural law simply equates "good" with "natural" and accepts the fallacy.
He argues that Moore's argument applies only to consequentialist theories, never to natural law.
He denies that Moore ever wrote about ethics.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what does natural law theory learn from Kantian ethics?

answers.text: That consequences are the only thing that ever matters morally.
That human nature has no bearing on ethics whatsoever.
That all moral prohibitions must be abandoned in favor of pure calculation.
That intentions matter, not just outcomes; the Doctrine of Double Effect reflects the same intuition behind Kant's distinction between acting from duty and merely in accordance with duty.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what does natural law theory learn from virtue ethics?

answers.text: That moral knowledge alone is sufficient for reliable right action, with no need for character formation.

That stable dispositions of character (the virtues) are needed to translate moral knowledge into reliable action, since knowledge without virtue leaves a person unable to reliably act on natural law precepts.
That virtue ethics and natural law theory are entirely incompatible and share no common ground.
That the doctrine of the mean replaces the doctrine of double effect.

questions.text: According to the lesson's four-theory map, what is natural law theory's starting question?

answers.text: What produces the best outcomes?
What does duty require?
What kind of person should I be?
What is genuinely good for human beings?

questions.text: According to the lesson's four-theory map, what is the key objection to consequentialism?

answers.text: It cannot explain why individual persons may not be sacrificed for the aggregate good.
It generates implausible results in hard cases such as the lying murderer.
It does not fully explain why the human telos has normative force.
It cannot explain the is-ought gap.

questions.text: According to the lesson's four-theory map, what does deontology (Kant) need from the other theories?

answers.text: Natural law's account of what grounds the human telos.
The consequentialist reminder that outcomes matter, and the virtue account of practical wisdom to handle hard cases.
The virtue-theoretic account of how moral knowledge becomes reliable in action.
The Kantian insight that persons have inviolable dignity.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what does Socrates mean, in the Apology, by saying "the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being"?

answers.text: That most people should not bother pursuing philosophy at all.
That anyone who has not studied formal logic cannot live a meaningful life.
That Socrates regretted his own life and considered it not worth living.
That human beings, as rational animals, are capable of an examined life lived in the light of reason reflecting on what is genuinely good, which mere living does not exhaust.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what does the course claim is the most important thing it has tried to give students, more than any specific set of answers?

answers.text: A single settled answer to the question of how one should live.
A comprehensive list of every philosopher who has ever written about ethics.

The habit of persistently asking what is genuinely at stake, whose interests are affected, what duties apply, and what kind of person an action will make you, a habit the tradition calls practical wisdom.
A guarantee that moral disagreement can always be resolved through calculation.

discussions.title: 1.01 · Your Own Euthyphro Moment
discussions.html:
Content Focus

Plato's Euthyphro stages the first systematic philosophical encounter in the Western tradition: a man who claims moral certainty is asked to define what he knows, and the definition collapses. This assignment asks you to undergo the same test yourself. By applying Socratic questioning to a moment of your own moral certainty, you practice the foundational skill of the course: turning a conviction into an argument and evaluating whether it holds.

Focus Question

When you feel morally certain about something, what standard are you actually relying on? Can you define it precisely enough to survive Socratic questioning?

Primary Source Preparation

Before writing your post, complete the following in your course notebook:

  1. Read the opening exchange of Plato's Euthyphro through 12e.
  2. Identify at least two definitions of piety that Euthyphro offers.
  3. For each definition, write one sentence explaining why Socrates finds it insufficient.

Notebook preparation is not submitted separately, but your discussion post should reflect that you did it.

Your Assignment

Write a discussion post that does the following three things:

  1. Describe a situation in which you felt morally certain about something. Be specific: name the situation clearly enough that a reader understands what was at stake.
  2. Apply Socrates' question to yourself. What definition or standard were you relying on? State it as precisely as you can.
  3. Evaluate whether your standard holds up. Using the same kind of questioning Socrates applies to Euthyphro, does your definition survive? If it collapses, explain how. If it holds, explain why.

Success Criteria

A strong discussion post will:

  • Describe a specific situation, not a vague general principle
  • State the moral standard explicitly rather than leaving it implied
  • Apply Socratic questioning in a way that reflects the Euthyphro reading
  • Reach a genuine conclusion about whether the standard survives
  • Write in a scholarly register appropriate to a philosophy course

Submitting Your Work

Post your response to this discussion. You do not need a title. Aim for a length that covers all three parts of the prompt fully: most strong responses fall between 200 and 350 words. Read at least one classmate's post and respond with a follow-up Socratic question.
